title: Paint and brooms — the me- prefix, part 2
goal: Complete the *me-* prefix: *meny-* for roots in *s*, *menge-* for one-syllable roots, plain *me-* before *l, m, n, r, w, y*. Then learn the spoken forms (*nyapu, nulis, ngambil, ngecat*) that you hear far more often than the written ones.
bekal: build *meny-*, *menge-* and plain *me-* verbs: *menyapu, mengecat, melihat*
turn any written *me-* verb into its spoken form: *menyiram → nyiram, mengepel → ngepel*
talk about housework and repairs, and deal with a *tukang*

notes: **Tukang langganan** — a *tukang* is a skilled tradesman: *tukang cat* (painter), *tukang kayu* (carpenter), *tukang listrik* (electrician). *Langganan* means "regular": your regular handyman, your regular vegetable seller. A trusted *tukang* is worth more than any hardware shop.

**Mengecat** — *cat* (paint) has only one syllable, so instead of a plain nasal the prefix becomes *menge-*. Pak Min's *ngecat* is the spoken version. It works the same with *cek*, from English "check": *mengecek*, spoken *ngecek*.

**Putih tulang**, literally "bone white", is off-white. Indonesian colour names love comparisons: *merah bata* (brick red), *biru langit* (sky blue), *hijau daun* (leaf green), and *abu-abu* (grey, from *abu*, ash).

**Lembap, jamur, bocor** — damp, mould, leaking: the three words every tenant in the tropics learns in the first rainy season. ⚠️ The standard spelling is *lembap*; you will often see *lembab*, which the dictionary treats as non-standard.

**Lusa baru ngecat** — *baru* after a time word means "not until then": *Lusa baru ngecat* is "I won't paint until the day after tomorrow". It is the same *baru* as in Unit 1's *baru dua hari*, seen from the other side.

**Biar nggak kena cat** — *biar* is spoken "so that" (standard *supaya* or *agar*, Unit 12). *Kena* is "to be hit by, get caught by": *kena hujan* (caught in the rain), *kena macet* (stuck in traffic), *kena cat* (get paint on it).

grammars.title: meny- and plain me-
body: Roots in *s* lose the *s* and take *meny-*: one more case of the swallowed sound. Roots in *l, m, n, r, w, y* (and *ny*) need no nasal at all, so the prefix is a bare *me-*.
after: As with *p, t, k*, the *s* drops only before a vowel: *sewa → menyewa* (to rent), but a cluster stays, as in *mensponsori* (to sponsor).
⚠️ Don't double the *m*: it is *memasak*, not *mem-masak*, and *merawat*, not *mer-rawat*. The prefix just sits in front of the root.

grammars.title: menge-: roots of one syllable
body: A handful of short roots, mostly borrowed, have only one syllable. They take *menge-*, which gives the verb enough body to be pronounced comfortably.
after: *Menge-* also tells you something when you read: whenever you see it, the root is a single syllable, so *mengebom* must come from *bom* (bomb).
The spoken forms simply keep the *nge-*. Of all the *me-* verbs, these are the ones people most often say in full, because *ngecat* and *mengecat* are both easy to pronounce.

dialogs.intro: Monday morning at the office. Mas Bayu, coffee in hand, asks Sarah how her weekend went.

notes: **Kok kayak pembaca berita, sih?** *Kayak* is spoken *seperti* (like), and *kok … sih* together turn a question into friendly teasing. Nobody minds being told they sound like the news: it means your grammar is right.
**Kaku** means "stiff": of joints, of manners, and of language. Full *me-* verbs in a chat about housework are correct but *kaku*, rather like saying "I then proceeded to sweep" in English.
**Nyapu, ngepel, nyiram** — spoken verbs keep only the nasal: *menyapu → nyapu*, *mengepel → ngepel*, *menyiram → nyiram*. The grammar box below shows how to make them from any root.

**Itu baru orang Jogja!** This *baru* means "now that's a real…": *Ini baru kopi!* (now this is coffee!). **Jogja** and **Yogya** are the same city: *Yogyakarta* is the official name, *Jogja* is what locals say and what the tourist board prints.

**Jadi ngecat?** At the start of a sentence *jadi* means "so", but after a subject it means "to go ahead as planned": *Jadi ke Bali?* (still going to Bali?) — *Jadi.* (Yes.) *Nggak jadi* means "called off".
**Mantap!** is "great, solid, top", everywhere among young men and on social media. Bayu's warning is real advice: spoken nasal forms in a work email look as careless as "gonna" in an English one.

grammars.title: The spoken forms
body: Speech keeps the nasal and throws away the *me*. Once you know the written verb, the spoken one is automatic.
after: Roots in *b, d, g, j* and *l, m, r, w* usually just go bare in speech: *beli, dengar, jual, lihat, masak*. Roots in *c* take an irregular *ny-*: *nyari*, *nyuci* (to wash).
💬 In Jakarta you will also hear *nge-* in front of all sorts of roots: *ngegambar*, *ngeganggu* (to bother). Recognise it for now; Unit 19 is all about Jakarta speech.
A useful habit: when you hear a spoken form, rebuild the written one in your head (*ngambil → mengambil → ambil*). That is also how you find the word in a dictionary.

blocks.text: Housework is where you will hear spoken nasal forms most. Learn each verb in all three shapes: the root you look up, the form you write, and the form you say.

blocks.title: Working with a tukang
items: A *tukang* is paid by the day (*harian*) or for the whole job (*borongan*). Agree which before any work starts.
Offer drinks and a snack: *teh manis* or coffee with some *gorengan* (fritters), mid-morning and mid-afternoon, is ordinary courtesy.
*Tukang cat* painter, *tukang kayu* carpenter, *tukang listrik* electrician, *tukang ledeng* plumber, *tukang las* welder.
Ask on day one who buys the *bahan* (materials): *Bahannya siapa yang beli, Pak?* Often it is you, with the *tukang* telling you what and where.

blocks.text: Plus the special case: one-syllable roots take *menge-* (*cat → mengecat*). The four sounds that drop are easy to remember as *KaTa SaPu*: *k, t, s, p*.

items: *pakai → memakai*, *tulis → menulis*, *sapu → menyapu*, *kirim → mengirim*: the four droppers.
*beli → membeli*, *dengar → mendengar*, *ganti → mengganti*: the nasal is added, nothing is lost.
*lihat → melihat*, *rawat → merawat*: no nasal at all.
